2.title: Justified by Faith: The Gospel Confronts the Church
2.overview:
Chapter 2 is the biographical argument’s climax and the letter’s theological turning point. Two episodes dominate: the Jerusalem conference (vv. 1–10), where the apostles affirmed Paul’s gospel of grace without requiring Gentile circumcision; and the Antioch confrontation (vv. 11–14), where Paul opposed Peter to his face because Peter’s behavior contradicted the gospel he believed. Both episodes illustrate the same point: the gospel of justification by faith alone is the non-negotiable centre of Christianity, and it must be defended even when the offender is the most respected leader in the church.

The chapter’s second half (vv. 15–21) is the theological centrepiece of the entire letter — the most concentrated statement of justification by faith in Paul’s letters apart from Romans 3. “A person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ.” The verb “justified” (dikaioō) is a forensic term: to be declared righteous by the divine judge, to have one’s legal status before God established as “not guilty.” This declaration is made not on the basis of law-keeping (which can only expose and condemn sin) but on the basis of faith in Jesus Christ.

The chapter ends with the most luminous personal testimony in Paul’s letters: “I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.” This is the gospel arriving at its destination: not merely a changed legal status but a transformed life — union with Christ, the old self crucified, the new life animated by faith in the one who loved and gave himself for me, personally, individually, sacrificially.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Paul Accepted by the Apostles
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1 opens with a number that is itself the argument: after fourteen years of preaching and planting without Jerusalem laying a hand on his message. He goes up with Barnabas, who had once vouched for him when the Jerusalem church would not go near him, and with Titus, an uncircumcised Greek — not a companion so much as an exhibit. In v. 2 he goes because of a revelation, not by summons, and meets the leaders privately rather than staging a public showdown he could have won.

His stated purpose, to make sure he was not running in vain, is easily misread as doubt about his gospel; chapter 1 forbids that. The danger he is guarding against is that the church might become two churches, a circumcised one and an uncircumcised one, each with its own apostle and its own terms.

Verse 3 gives the verdict in one line: even Titus, who was with me, was not forced to be circumcised, though he was a Greek. With the test case standing in the room, Jerusalem did not require him to become a Jew. Verses 4–5 explain the pressure that made this a fight. The language is the language of espionage — false brothers secretly brought in, men who slipped in to spy out the freedom of the Gentile churches, whose stated object was slavery. Paul did not yield even for a moment, and gives a pastoral reason rather than a principled one: so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved for you. Doctrinal firmness is a man standing in a doorway so that people behind him can stay free.

Verse 6 reports the outcome in two words — they added nothing to me — and grounds it in the fact that God shows no partiality, a principle Paul turns on the apostles themselves. Verses 7–8 set out the shape of the agreement: Paul entrusted with the gospel to the uncircumcised just as Peter to the circumcised, one gospel and two mission fields, with God himself named as the one who worked through both men. In v. 9 the order of the clauses carries the theology: the pillars first perceived the grace that was given and only then gave the right hand of fellowship — recognition of what God had done, not a handshake that conferred it. And v. 10 adds the single request Jerusalem made, that they remember the poor, which Paul was already eager to do.
verseByVerse.theology:
One Gospel, One People, One Way In

The Titus decision of v. 3 settles a question of the first order: justification is on identical terms for Jew and Gentile, and no covenant marker supplements faith at the point of acceptance with God. This is not a statement about cultural inclusion; it is a claim about the nature of justification itself, and the Reformed understanding of the covenant of grace — one covenant, one people, one Saviour, one way of entry — finds its clearest apostolic expression here.

Two further principles sit inside the passage. The word entrusted (v. 7) is a steward’s word, and it quietly disqualifies everyone in the dispute from editing the message: Paul may not adjust it to suit Gentiles and Jerusalem may not adjust it to suit Jews, for the same reason, which is that neither owns it. And the sequence of v. 9 — grace perceived, then fellowship extended — gives the church its permanent task in recognising anyone. Ordination does not manufacture a minister and a handshake does not manufacture a brother. The church perceives what God has given and says so.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Galatia was being told that Gentile believers needed circumcision added to their faith. Paul’s answer is that he took this precise question to Jerusalem with an uncircumcised Greek at his side (vv. 1–3), and the men whose authority the Judaizers were invoking added nothing (v. 6) and shook his hand (v. 9). The Judaizers are not following the Jerusalem apostles; they are contradicting them.

Now: A reader who knows Acts will ask why Paul later circumcised Timothy (Acts 16:3) if he would not let anyone touch Titus. The answer draws the line exactly where vv. 3–5 draw it: Timothy’s mother was Jewish and nobody was demanding it as a condition of salvation, so it was free, and Paul did it for the sake of getting into synagogues. With Titus the same act was being required. Anything may be done for the gospel; nothing may be added to it. The same test still sorts real questions from false ones. Where a practice is offered as helpful, Christians may differ; where it is required for full acceptance, the gospel is at stake. And v. 10 guards the other flank: having refused to add one item to the gospel, Paul accepts an obligation to the poor without a murmur, because that is not an addition but what grace does once it has arrived.

verseByVerse.quote: Then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus along with me. I went up because of a revelation and set before them (though privately before those who seemed influential) the gospel that I proclaim among the Gentiles, in order to make sure I was not running or had not run in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is still counting years, and the number is the argument. After fourteen years — fourteen more years of preaching, planting, and being run out of towns, without the Jerusalem apostles laying a hand on his message. If his gospel had needed their sign-off, it had been operating without it for the better part of two decades, and it had been working.

Then three details, each doing a job.

With Barnabas, taking Titus along with me. Barnabas is the man who had vouched for Paul when the Jerusalem church would not go near him. Titus is a Greek, uncircumcised, and Paul walks him into the middle of a meeting about whether Greeks must be circumcised. He is not carrying a companion. He is carrying an exhibit.

I went up because of a revelation. Not because he was summoned, not because his nerve had failed. He was sent, by the same authority that had sent him everywhere else.

Though privately before those who seemed influential. He went to the leadership first, in a closed room, rather than staging a confrontation in front of a crowd. It is worth noticing what a man who is right does with his rightness here. He could have forced a public showdown and won it. He chose the room where a thing can be settled instead of the platform where a thing gets performed.

And then a phrase that has troubled readers for centuries: those who seemed influential — the Greek is hoi dokountes, literally the ones who seem, the ones held in repute. It sounds like a sneer, and Paul is certainly not overawed. But he is not attacking Peter and James; he will call them pillars in a few verses and shake their hands. He is refusing one thing only: the idea that reputation is what makes a gospel true. The Judaizers had been trading on Jerusalem’s prestige. Paul will grant Jerusalem everything except the right to be the reason.

In order to make sure I was not running or had not run in vain. This is the line most likely to be misread, because it sounds as if Paul had doubts about his message and went to have them settled. He did not, and the whole of chapter 1 forbids that reading. The danger he is guarding against is not that his gospel might turn out to be false. It is that the church might turn out to be two churches — a circumcised one and an uncircumcised one, each with its own apostle and its own terms — and if that happened, everything he had built would come apart in a generation. He is not checking his doctrine. He is protecting the unity that his doctrine requires.

One historical question arises here, and since honest scholars land in different places it is worth stating plainly rather than glossing over. Which visit to Jerusalem is this? Acts records several. Many take it to be the Jerusalem Council of Acts 15, where exactly this question was decided. Others take it to be the earlier famine-relief visit of Acts 11:30, which would mean Galatians was written before the Council ever met. The second view has one strong argument in its favour: Paul describes a private meeting, whereas Acts 15 was a public assembly — and if a formal apostolic ruling on circumcision already existed, it is very hard to explain why Paul, fighting for his life on precisely that issue, never once quotes it.

Nothing in the letter’s argument depends on settling it, and a reader may hold it loosely. What matters is what Paul says happened in that room, and he is about to tell us in one sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: But even Titus, who was with me, was not forced to be circumcised, though he was a Greek. Yet because of false brothers secretly brought in—who slipped in to spy out our freedom that we have in Christ Jesus, so that they might bring us into slavery— to them we did not yield in submission even for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything came down to one man standing in the room, and whether anybody would reach for a knife.

But even Titus, who was with me, was not forced to be circumcised, though he was a Greek. That is the verdict, and Paul reports it in a single line because a single line is all it needs. The apostles looked at an uncircumcised Gentile believer and did not require him to become a Jew. If the Judaizers were right, Jerusalem had a duty to say so with Titus standing there. Jerusalem said nothing of the kind.

A fair question comes up here, and a reader who knows Acts will feel it immediately. Paul later took Timothy and circumcised him (Acts 16:3). How is that not the very thing he refused here?

The difference is everything. Timothy’s mother was a Jewish believer (Acts 16:1), so he was already reckoned a Jew by birth and had simply never been marked as one; and nobody was demanding it as a condition of his salvation. Paul did it so that Timothy could get into synagogues and preach. Titus was a Gentile, and the demand was being made as a requirement of acceptance with God. So the rule Paul is working by is not that circumcision is forbidden. It is that anything may be done for the sake of the gospel, and nothing may be added to it. The moment a thing stops being free and starts being necessary, Paul will die on that hill — and the same man who circumcised Timothy would not let anyone touch Titus.

Then the sentence turns dark. Because of false brothers secretly brought in — who slipped in to spy out our freedom that we have in Christ Jesus, so that they might bring us into slavery. The vocabulary is the vocabulary of espionage. They were brought in alongside, the word used of smuggling something in under cover; they slipped in like men getting over a wall at night; they came to spy out, the word for reconnoitring an enemy position. These were not honest men with a different opinion who lost an argument. They came to gather intelligence on how free the Gentile churches actually were, and to report back.

And Paul names their object without softening it: so that they might bring us into slavery. That is the whole letter in four words. What was on offer looked like a promotion — full membership, proper standing, the marks of the covenant. What it actually was, was chains. Anything that makes acceptance with God depend on a performance puts a man back on a treadmill he cannot get off, because the performance is never finished and the verdict is never in.

To them we did not yield in submission even for a moment. Not an hour of diplomatic concession. Not a temporary accommodation to be revisited when tempers cooled. It is a strange thing to praise a man for, until you notice what compromise looks like from the inside: it never presents itself as surrender, only as a small, reasonable, temporary allowance for the sake of peace. Paul knew what the first inch was worth.

And then he says why, and it is the most pastoral sentence in the paragraph: so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved for you. Not so that Paul might win. Not for the principle of the thing. For you — for a congregation of Gentile converts hundreds of miles away who would never know the meeting had happened.

That is what doctrinal firmness is for, and it is worth saying to anyone who finds Paul’s tone in this letter hard to like. He is not a man who enjoys a fight. He is a man standing in a doorway so that people behind him can stay free, and the freedom of every Gentile believer since — including the freedom of whoever is reading this — came down that corridor.

verseByVerse.quote: And from those who seemed to be influential (what they were makes no difference to me; God shows no partiality)—those, I say, who seemed influential added nothing to me. On the contrary, when they saw that I had been entrusted with the gospel to the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been entrusted with the gospel to the circumcised (for he who worked through Peter for his apostolic ministry to the circumcised worked also through me for mine to the Gentiles),
verseByVerse.commentary:
Added nothing to me. Two words in Greek, and they end the argument.

The Judaizers’ case rested on the claim that Paul’s gospel was incomplete — that the men in Jerusalem had the full version and Paul had been handing out an abridgement. So Paul reports the outcome of the meeting in the bluntest possible terms. The pillars of the Jerusalem church heard his gospel in full, and they had nothing to add to it. No correction. No supplement. No condition attached. Whatever the Galatians were being told is missing, the men supposedly missing it did not think so.

What they were makes no difference to me; God shows no partiality. That last phrase is a quotation of sorts — the Old Testament says repeatedly that God does not lift up faces, does not take the important man’s side because he is important (Deut. 10:17; 2 Chr. 19:7). Paul turns it on the apostles themselves. Peter had walked with Jesus and Paul had not, and it makes no difference to the question, because God is not impressed by curricula vitae. It is a dangerous principle to hold and a liberating one: the same God who is unimpressed by Peter’s credentials is unimpressed by anyone else’s, which means nobody in the room outranks the truth.

Then the reason they added nothing, and it is not that they were persuaded by Paul’s arguments. When they saw that I had been entrusted with the gospel to the uncircumcised. They looked at the evidence. Something had plainly been happening in the Gentile world, and it was not Paul’s doing.

The word is entrusted — the language of a steward handed something that belongs to someone else. It is worth pausing on, because it quietly settles the entire dispute. A man entrusted with a message has no authority to revise it; that is what entrusting means. Paul cannot edit this gospel to please Gentiles and Jerusalem cannot edit it to please Jews, for exactly the same reason. Neither of them owns it.

And the parallel he draws is careful: he was entrusted with the gospel to the uncircumcised just as Peter had been entrusted with the gospel to the circumcised. One gospel, two mission fields. Not two gospels, and not a senior apostle with a junior assistant.

Then verse 8, in brackets, and the brackets hide the best sentence in the paragraph: for he who worked through Peter for his apostolic ministry to the circumcised worked also through me for mine to the Gentiles.

Notice the subject. It is not Peter who worked, and not Paul. There is a third party in that sentence and he is the only one doing anything. The same God energised both ministries; Peter and Paul are the instruments through which he worked. Which is why the comparison never becomes a competition. Two men were used, and one God was working, and the results in Jerusalem and the results in Galatia have precisely the same author.

There is a quiet mercy in that for anyone who has ever measured his own ministry against somebody else’s and come away discouraged — the teacher whose class is small beside the one whose hall is full, the parent whose children came slowly to faith beside the family where it all seemed easy. The verse does not say the two men were equally gifted. It says one God was at work in both. He is not divided among his servants, spending himself heavily on the impressive ones and thinly on the rest. The whole of him works in each.

verseByVerse.quote: and when James and Cephas and John, who seemed to be pillars, perceived the grace that was given to me, they gave the right hand of fellowship to Barnabas and me, that we should go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised. Only, they asked us to remember the poor, the very thing I was eager to do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Watch the order of this sentence, because the order is the point.

They did not shake hands and then discover the grace. When James and Cephas and John, who seemed to be pillars, perceived the grace that was given to me, they gave the right hand of fellowship to Barnabas and me. First they saw the grace; then they extended the hand. The recognition came first and the fellowship followed from it, and if the clauses are put the other way round the theology quietly changes — as though the handshake conferred something. It did not. It acknowledged something God had already done.

That is the pattern for how the church recognises anything. Ordination does not manufacture a minister and a handshake does not manufacture a brother. The church’s task is to perceive what God has given and then say so publicly. Where grace is evidently at work, the only faithful response is to acknowledge it — and where it is not, no ceremony will supply it.

Pillars. James, Cephas and John — and the picture is architectural: the men on whom the weight rests. The James here is not the apostle John’s brother, who had already been executed by Herod (Acts 12:2), but the Lord’s brother, the one who had not believed during the ministry and now leads the Jerusalem church.

The right hand of fellowship. It is the oldest gesture there is, and it means the same thing in every century: an open right hand holds no weapon, and a man who gives it is saying that between us this is finished. The word behind fellowship is koinōnia, partnership — a joint stake in the same enterprise, not merely a truce.

Consider what actually happened in that room. The apostle who had been hunting Christians and the apostle who had denied Christ in a courtyard put their hands together over a gospel neither of them had earned, and agreed to spend their lives on it in different countries. Whatever else the church is, it is a company of forgiven enemies who have stopped competing for a standing that was never theirs to win. Nobody in that handshake had a record worth defending. That is what made it possible.

That we should go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised. A division of labour, not a division of message — and it was never watertight, since Peter opened the Gentile door in the first place (Acts 10) and Paul went to the synagogue in every town he entered.

Only, they asked us to remember the poor, the very thing I was eager to do.

One request. After a meeting about circumcision, the law, and the terms of salvation, the single thing Jerusalem asks is that the poor not be forgotten — and Paul says he was already straining at the leash to do it. He meant it. Years of his life went into the collection for the famine-struck believers in Judea, and he wrote whole chapters raising it (Rom. 15:25–27; 2 Cor. 8–9).

It is a striking place for the paragraph to land. Paul has just refused to add one item to the gospel, and immediately accepts an obligation to the poor without a murmur — because it is not an addition. Nothing has been placed between a sinner and God. What has been named is what grace does once it has arrived. A church that has understood justification by faith alone and has no interest in the hungry has not understood it. (cf. Jas. 2:15–17; 1 John 3:17)

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The scene shifts to Antioch, and the man just called a pillar is called wrong. In v. 11 Paul opposed him to his face — not privately, not by letter — because he stood condemned, a courtroom word in a tense that matters: Peter stood already condemned by the contradiction between what he believed and what he was doing. Paul did not pass the sentence; he read it out.

Verse 12 supplies the facts. Before certain men came from James, Peter was eating with the Gentiles — and a shared table in that world meant shared life and full acceptance, so Antioch had watched its most famous visitor live out the gospel in the most visible way available. When they arrived he drew back and separated himself, two verbs that are both gradual: no policy was announced, he simply began sitting elsewhere. And Paul names the cause without softening it: fearing the circumcision party. Not conviction. Peter had changed no opinion; he changed his seat because of who was watching. This is the apostle who had the vision on the rooftop and defended Gentile inclusion to the whole Jerusalem church (Acts 10–11), and who years earlier had denied his Lord to a servant girl. Fear of man is not a beginner’s sin that maturity leaves behind.

Verse 13 shows how fast it spread. The rest of the Jewish believers acted hypocritically — a theatre word, meaning to play a part one’s convictions do not support — and even Barnabas was led astray. The man who had vouched for Paul, fetched him out of Tarsus and been stoned at his side went with the current, and no argument is recorded anywhere in the passage. It took a few significant people sitting at another table.

Verse 14 gives Paul’s diagnosis and his rebuke. Their conduct was not in step with the truth of the gospel — a walking word; their doctrine was orthodox and their feet were wrong. The gospel can be denied by a seating plan as effectively as by a sermon. And the question he puts to Peter before them all closes every exit: if a Jew has been living like a Gentile, on what ground does he now force Gentiles to live like Jews? Nothing had been said out loud, which is the point of the word force. Pressure does not have to be spoken to be applied.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Gospel Governs the Feet, Not Only the Confession

Peter’s failure was not doctrinal. He had proclaimed the equality of Jew and Gentile before God and won the argument for it. What v. 14 exposes is a gap between a confession genuinely held and a life not walking in line with it — which is what hypocrisy means in Paul’s usage, not the cynical pretence of faith one does not have. The Reformers’ principle that the church is always to be reformed by the gospel bites here: the gospel must govern table habits, social pressure and power dynamics, not merely statements of faith.

There is a further point of some weight. Peter is treated in this passage as a fallible man who can be publicly withstood and corrected by another apostle on a matter of the gospel — and Scripture records it without embarrassment. Whatever authority the Jerusalem leadership had, it was never authority over the message, which is precisely the argument of vv. 6–9.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter’s withdrawal at Antioch was socially motivated, not theologically: v. 12 says he feared the circumcision party. It is the same snare Paul named at 1:10 — am I trying to please man? — and it swept up the whole Jewish contingent and Barnabas with it (v. 13).

Now: Two things in this section reach a reader directly. The first is a test anyone can run: most people have a room in which they are a slightly different Christian — the workplace where faith goes quiet, the family table where a conviction is not mentioned, the old friends around whom the language changes. Peter did not deny the gospel at Antioch; he moved to a different table when certain people were looking, and v. 11 calls that standing condemned.

The second is the question v. 14 always raises: should Christians confront leaders publicly? Usually not. The Lord’s instruction for sin between brothers is to go privately first (Matt. 18:15–17), and an accusation against an elder needs witnesses — though the same passage adds that those who persist in sin are to be rebuked before all (1 Tim. 5:19–20). Four things line up here and rarely all line up: the conduct was public, the matter was the gospel itself, others were already being carried away, and Paul said it to Peter’s face at cost to himself rather than about him afterwards to somebody else. That last is the test most often failed. And it did not end the friendship — an old man writing his final letter still called him our beloved brother Paul (2 Pet. 3:15–16).

verseByVerse.quote: But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he stood condemned. For before certain men came from James, he was eating with the Gentiles; but when they came he drew back and separated himself, fearing the circumcision party.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scene changes to Antioch, and the man who has just been called a pillar is about to be called wrong.

I opposed him to his face. Not a letter. Not a word with him afterwards. Not a delegation. Face to face, and as the next verses make clear, in front of everybody. The Greek phrase is as confrontational as it sounds in English, and the whole church was watching.

Because he stood condemned. The word is a courtroom word, and the tense matters: not that Paul condemned him, but that he stood already condemned — by his own behaviour, by the contradiction between what he believed and what he was doing. Paul did not pass the sentence. He read it out.

What had happened is described with painful precision. Before certain men came from James, he was eating with the Gentiles. Eating together was not a casual matter in that world. A shared table meant shared life, mutual acceptance, family. For a Jew to sit down to a Gentile meal was to declare that the wall had come down — and Peter had been doing it, meal after meal, which means the church at Antioch had watched their most famous visitor live out the gospel in the most visible way available.

But when they came he drew back and separated himself. Two verbs, and both are gradual. He drew back — a word used of a ship easing away from a quay, of a soldier giving ground. He separated himself. Nobody announced a policy. He simply began sitting elsewhere, and everyone knew what it meant.

Fearing the circumcision party. There it is, and Paul does not let anyone pretend otherwise. It was not conviction. Peter had not changed his mind about anything; he changed his seat because of who was watching.

Two things about this passage are worth facing rather than tidying.

The first is the question of how this was possible. This is the man who had the vision on the rooftop and heard the voice saying what God has made clean, do not call common; who walked into Cornelius’s house and watched the Spirit fall on Gentiles; who defended the whole thing to the Jerusalem church and won the argument (Acts 10–11). He was not under-informed. He was the leading expert in the room on precisely this point.

Which is the lesson, and it is a hard one. Knowing a truth and having settled it publicly does not immunise a man against abandoning it when the wrong people walk in. This is the same Peter who knew exactly who Jesus was and denied him to a servant girl beside a fire. The mechanism had not changed in twenty years: not doubt, not argument, but the sudden weight of a watching face. Fear of man is not a beginner’s sin that maturity leaves behind.

The second is the phrase certain men came from James, which has been used to blame James, and probably should not be. Luke records the Jerusalem church later writing to Antioch about men who had gone out and unsettled them although we gave them no instructions (Acts 15:24). Men who arrive claiming a great name are not always carrying it. What is certain is the effect: their arrival was enough, and Peter did not even wait to be asked.

A reader may test himself here more easily than he would like. Everyone has a room in which he is a slightly different Christian — the workplace where faith goes quiet, the family table where a conviction is not mentioned, the group of old friends where the language changes. Peter did not deny the gospel at Antioch. He simply moved to a different table when certain people were looking, and Paul calls that standing condemned.

verseByVerse.quote: And the rest of the Jews acted hypocritically along with him, so that even Barnabas was led astray by their hypocrisy. But when I saw that their conduct was not in step with the truth of the gospel, I said to Cephas before them all, “If you, though a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you force the Gentiles to live like Jews?”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The damage spreads in a single verse, and the name at the end of it is the one that hurts.

And the rest of the Jews acted hypocritically along with him. The word is hypokrisis, and it comes from the theatre — it is the word for playing a part, speaking lines that are not your own. Paul is not accusing these men of secret unbelief. He is saying they were acting: behaving in a way their convictions did not support because the audience had changed.

So that even Barnabas was led astray by their hypocrisy. Even Barnabas. The man whose name means son of encouragement. The man who had stood up for Paul when the whole Jerusalem church believed he was a plant, who had gone to Tarsus to fetch him out of obscurity, who had travelled the first missionary journey at his side and been stoned alongside him. If one man in Antioch could be counted on, it was Barnabas, and he was carried away too.

That detail is not there to shame Barnabas. It is there to show how strong the current was. It did not take an argument — nobody has recorded a single word of persuasion in this passage. It took a few significant people sitting at a different table, and the whole church moved.

When I saw that their conduct was not in step with the truth of the gospel. The verb is a walking word: they were not walking straight, not keeping to the line. And this is the sentence that gives the whole episode its weight. Paul does not say their doctrine was wrong. Their doctrine was fine; every man at those tables would have signed the same confession. Their feet were wrong. The gospel is not merely something to be believed accurately; it is something to be walked in, and it can be denied by a seating plan as effectively as by a sermon.

Then the rebuke itself: If you, though a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you force the Gentiles to live like Jews? It is a trap with no way out. Peter had been living freely, eating what Gentiles ate — so he plainly did not believe the food laws still bound him. Yet by withdrawing he was telling Gentile believers that if they wanted his company at the table, they would have to take on the very rules he himself had stopped keeping. Nobody had said this out loud. That is the force of the word force: pressure does not have to be spoken to be applied, and Gentile Christians in Antioch had just been shown, with no words at all, what it would cost them to be treated as brothers.

Which raises the practical question this passage always raises, and it deserves a straight answer rather than a shrug: does this mean a Christian should confront leaders publicly?

Usually not, and Scripture is careful about it. The Lord’s instruction for sin between brothers is to go privately first, and only widen the circle if there is no repentance (Matt. 18:15–17). Paul himself tells Timothy not to entertain an accusation against an elder except on two or three witnesses. But the same passage adds the other half: as for those who persist in sin, rebuke them in the presence of all (1 Tim. 5:19–20).

Four things line up here and they rarely all line up. The conduct was public, so a private word could not undo it. The matter was the gospel itself, not a preference or a personality. Others were already being swept away, Barnabas among them. And Paul said it to his face, in the room, at cost to himself — not about him, afterwards, to somebody else. That last one is the test most often failed. A great deal of what calls itself courage in the church is a message sent to a third party, or a post written about a man who will never be in the room. Paul’s way is harder and kinder: he said it where Peter could answer.

And it did not end the friendship. Years later, an old man writing his last letter mentioned our beloved brother Paul, and the wisdom given to him, and the parts of his letters that are hard to understand (2 Pet. 3:15–16). Peter took it. There is no bitterness anywhere in the record. Two men who both knew what it was to be forgiven could survive being told the truth.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Whether vv. 15–21 are still Paul’s speech to Peter or have become direct address to the Galatians is disputed; either way this is the letter’s defining statement. Verse 15 looks like throat-clearing and is actually the argument: we ourselves are Jews by birth and not Gentile sinners. Take the most advantaged religious people on earth — covenant, Scriptures, temple, a lifetime of training — and even they abandoned the attempt and trusted a crucified man. If the law could justify anyone, it would have justified them.

Verse 16 says the thing three times in one verse, because everything rests on it: a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ. To justify is a courtroom word — not to make someone good but to declare him in the right. Almost everyone instinctively pictures salvation in medical terms, as a cure that may or may not work; justification is the judge’s verdict, given whole and at the beginning. God does heal the sinner he acquits, but he does not acquit him because the healing is going well. Works of the law covers the visible markers that separated Jew from Gentile — the very issues on the Antioch table — and then reaches wider, since by works of the law no one will be justified. The law is a mirror, and a mirror has never washed a face.

Verse 17 raises the standing objection: if grace is this free, has Christ made law-keepers into sinners and become a servant of sin? Paul’s certainly not is the strongest negative he owns. Verses 18–19 answer it. To rebuild what he tore down would be the real transgression — a man who demolishes an unsound building and then re-erects it stone by stone has declared the demolition to be the crime, which is exactly what Peter had begun doing one meal at a time. And through the law I died to the law: the law itself was the instrument, raising the standard until it convicted him, doing precisely what God gave it to do.

Verse 20 is the summit. I have been crucified with Christ — a completed event with standing results, since Christ died as a representative. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me does not mean Paul was erased; the next clause says the life I now live, and this is the most personality-drenched letter in the New Testament. What died was the self that had to be somebody. He lives in the flesh — in the body, on ordinary Mondays — and by faith rather than by sensation. Then the grammar goes singular: who loved me and gave himself for me. Verse 21 closes with the reductio: if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose. Christ plus performance says, underneath itself, that his performance was insufficient, and the cross does not survive being called a supplement.
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification by Faith: The Article by Which the Church Stands or Falls

Luther called justification by faith articulus stantis et cadentis ecclesiae, the article by which the church stands or falls, and vv. 15–21 are the classic passage for it. Justification is forensic — a declaration of status, not an infusion of goodness, though transformation certainly follows. It is by faith alone, its object is Christ alone, and it is by grace alone; and the Reformed tradition has always insisted the three stand or fall together. If faith is not the exclusive instrument, it is not by grace; if Christ is not the exclusive object of faith, it is not grace either.

One point of translation deserves noting since a reader may meet it. The phrase rendered faith in Jesus Christ in v. 16 can also be read as the faithfulness of Jesus Christ — his own obedience to the cross as the ground of acceptance. There is real truth in that reading. The majority Reformed rendering takes it as faith directed toward him, supported by the next clause, so we also have believed in Christ Jesus, which would be redundant otherwise. Either way the substance holds: the doing is his and the receiving is ours, and even the receiving contributes nothing. Faith is not a work that earns the verdict; it is the empty hand that takes it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Jewish believers had every religious advantage and still came the same way as the Gentiles they were now refusing to eat with (v. 15). The argument from the insider to the outsider is conclusive: if the law cannot justify those to whom it was given, it will not justify anyone else. And v. 18 lands directly on Antioch, where stones were going back into a wall that had been pulled down.

Now: The person who comes to faith from a life of moral respectability and the person who comes from obvious wreckage stand on identical ground, with the same righteousness, which is Christ’s. The respectability is as irrelevant to the verdict as the wreckage. There is a test in v. 16 that can be run on any ordinary week: ask what would have to be true for God to be pleased with you by Friday. If the honest answer requires a better performance than this week’s, something other than Christ is being trusted — and the verdict was never waiting on Friday.

Verse 20 answers a second worry. People who love that verse sometimes expect it to feel like something and are troubled when it does not. Paul does not claim a sensation of Christ’s presence; he says he lives by faith, trusting a person he cannot see on days when nothing is felt at all. The indwelling is a fact about where Christ is, not a report on how the believer is doing. And v. 19 speaks to anyone worn out by religious striving: the sense that it is never enough, that a good week is only a reprieve, is not a malfunction. It is the law doing its work, and its work is the last kindness of a schoolmaster who means to hand the pupil to someone else.

verseByVerse.quote: We ourselves are Jews by birth and not Gentile sinners; yet we know that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, so we also have believed in Christ Jesus, in order to be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no one will be justified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the sentence the Reformation was built on, and the letter’s own centre of gravity: a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ. Paul says it, then says it again, then says it a third time inside one verse, because everything else stands on it.

The word to get clear is justified, and it is not a word most people use on a Tuesday. It is a courtroom word. To justify is not to make someone good; it is to declare someone to be in the right. A judge who justifies a defendant does not improve him or treat him or educate him. He pronounces a verdict, and the man walks out of the court with a status he did not have when he walked in.

That distinction is worth holding onto, because almost everyone instinctively thinks of salvation in medical terms — God as a physician gradually curing us, with heaven at the end if the treatment works. Justification is not the doctor’s slow progress; it is the judge’s verdict, given whole, in a moment, and given at the beginning rather than the end. God does also heal the sinner he acquits, and that work goes on for a lifetime. But he does not acquit him because the healing is going well.

And the ground of that verdict is the whole quarrel. Works of the law means, first, the deeds the law of Moses required — and particularly the visible markers that separated Jew from Gentile: circumcision, the food rules, the holy days. Those were the exact issues on the table in Antioch. But Paul’s conclusion is wider than the markers, and the last clause shows it: by works of the law no one will be justified. No one. Not the Gentile without the law, and not the Pharisee who kept it better than his peers.

The reason is not that the law is a bad thing. Paul will insist later that it is holy and was given by God for good purposes. The reason is that the law is a mirror, and a mirror has never washed a face. It was given to show what righteousness looks like and, in showing it, to show a man what he is not.

Which is the force of verse 15, easily skipped as throat-clearing: we ourselves are Jews by birth and not Gentile sinners. Paul is not boasting; he is reasoning. Take the most advantaged religious people on earth — the covenant, the Scriptures, the temple, the sacrifices, a lifetime of training — and what did they do? We also have believed in Christ Jesus, in order to be justified by faith. The insiders had to come the same way as the outsiders. If the law could have justified anybody, it would have justified them, and instead they abandoned the attempt and trusted a crucified man.

One point of translation should be mentioned, since a reader may meet it and wonder. The phrase rendered faith in Jesus Christ can also be read as the faithfulness of Jesus Christ — meaning it is Christ’s own perfect obedience, all the way to the cross, that justifies. There is real truth in that: his faithfulness is indeed the ground on which anyone stands. But the majority Reformed reading takes it as our faith directed toward him, and the very next clause supports it — so we also have believed in Christ Jesus, which would be an odd thing to add if the point had just been made. Either way the verse says the same thing in the end. The doing is his; the receiving is ours, and even the receiving is not a contribution. Faith is not a work that earns the verdict. It is the empty hand that takes it.

There is a test in this that can be run on any ordinary week. Ask what would have to be true for God to be pleased with you by Friday. If the honest answer involves a better performance than this week’s, then something is being trusted that is not Christ — and the good news is that the verdict was never waiting on Friday. It was handed down at the cross and received by faith, and it does not move. (cf. Rom. 3:20–24; Phil. 3:8–9)

verseByVerse.quote: But if, in our endeavor to be justified in Christ, we too were found to be sinners, is Christ then a servant of sin? Certainly not!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul stops to answer an objection, and it is the objection this doctrine has always attracted.

The argument runs like this. If a man is accepted by God on the basis of faith rather than obedience, then his obedience does not finally matter — and look at what actually follows. Jewish believers who came to Christ stopped keeping the food laws and started eating with Gentiles. By the law’s reckoning they became sinners in the process. So Christ has taken observant men and made them law-breakers. Is he then a servant of sin — not merely tolerating it but actively promoting it, running errands for it?

Paul’s reply is the most violent negative in his vocabulary. Certainly not. The Greek is mē genoito, the phrase he reaches for when a suggestion is not to be weighed but thrown out of the room: may it never be, God forbid, perish the thought.

The charge deserves better than a shrug, though, and Paul answers it properly over the next several verses. But the shape of the answer is already in the way he frames the question. Notice what he does not say. He does not say that grace makes sin unimportant, and he does not deny that a justified person is still a sinner. He says something more careful: the fault cannot possibly lie where the objection puts it. Whatever is wrong when a believer sins, it is not that Christ put him up to it.

And there is a reason that is more than logic. To call Christ a servant of sin is to say something about the character of the one who died to destroy it — the man who took the whole weight of it into his own body and went into the dark under it. The objection is not merely mistaken; it is an insult to a person, and Paul reacts the way anyone reacts when someone slanders a friend who is not there to answer.

This objection has followed the doctrine of free grace ever since, and it always will. Paul faced it in Rome too, and put it more sharply: are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? (Rom. 6:1). It is a compliment of a strange sort. If a preacher has never once been accused of making grace too free, it is worth asking whether he has actually preached it — because Paul, who was preaching it exactly right, got accused constantly.

The answer he gives in Romans is the answer he is about to give here, and it is not a retreat into rule-keeping. It is a question about what happened to the person. Grace does not leave a sinner where it found him and merely change his paperwork. It puts him to death and raises him, and a man who has died to something does not go back to it as though nothing occurred. That is where the next three verses are going, and it is why the argument ends up at a cross rather than at a code of conduct.

verseByVerse.quote: For if I rebuild what I tore down, I prove myself to be a transgressor. For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Paul answers the objection, and he answers it about himself, in the first person, with a picture.

If I rebuild what I tore down, I prove myself to be a transgressor.

Picture a man who has spent years constructing a building, stone by stone, and has finally looked at it, judged it unsound, and pulled it down. Now imagine him going back and putting every stone up again. He has not merely wasted his time. He has publicly declared that the demolition was the crime.

What Paul tore down was the whole structure of acceptance by performance — the life he describes in chapter 1, advancing beyond his peers, zealous for the traditions, building a righteousness of his own. He took it apart when he met Christ. And this is the answer to the man who says grace makes sinners: the transgression would not be in leaving the law behind, it would be in going back to it. If he rebuilds that system, he condemns himself either way. Either he was wrong to pull it down, or he is wrong to put it up. What he cannot claim is that reconstruction is obedience.

And there is a direct application to Antioch in it, which is surely why he uses the first person so pointedly. Peter had been living in the freedom of the gospel and had begun laying stones back in place, one meal at a time.

Then verse 19, which is one of the strangest and best sentences in the letter: For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God.

Through the law. Not in spite of it, not by escaping it — the law itself was the instrument of his death to the law. That sounds like a riddle until one watches how it works. The law came to a man doing rather well and kept raising the standard until it had him. It said: not just murder, but anger; not just adultery, but the look; not just the deed, but the desire. And it kept saying it until the promising young Pharisee understood that he was not ahead of his peers at all, that the machine he had trusted had been designed to convict him, and that on those terms he was a dead man. So the law did precisely what God gave it to do. It killed him. And it killed him so that he could stop trying to live by it.

There is no gentler road to grace than this one, and it is worth saying honestly, because it is where many people actually are. Nobody comes to Christ while his own account still looks solvent. The ache underneath religious striving — the sense that it is never enough, that the standard keeps moving, that a good week is only ever a reprieve — is not a malfunction. It is the law doing its work, and its work is not cruelty. It is the last kindness of a schoolmaster who intends to hand the pupil over to someone else.

So that I might live to God. That is what the whole demolition was for. Not to leave a man in the rubble, but to get him out from under a life spent proving himself, and into a life lived toward God — which is the only kind of life the rubble was ever in the way of.

verseByVerse.quote: I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the summit of the letter, and one of the best-loved verses in the New Testament, and it begins with a funeral.

I have been crucified with Christ. The tense is one English does not carry well: a thing done in the past whose results stand permanently in the present. Not I am dying daily and not I try to crucify myself. It happened. It is finished. When Christ died, Paul died — because Christ died as a representative, the way Adam acted for a race, so that what happened to him happened to everyone joined to him.

Crucifixion is a deliberate word to choose. It was not a dignified death or a private one. Paul could have said he died with Christ; he says he was crucified, which is what you do to a criminal in public with nothing left of his standing. The old self — the impressive one, the one with the record and the achievements and the rising reputation in Judaism — did not retire honourably. It was executed.

It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me.

A careful reader stops here, and should, because taken alone the sentence sounds as if Paul has been erased — as if becoming a Christian means being emptied out and replaced, personality and all. Two things forbid that reading. The first is the very next clause, where Paul says the life I now live — there is plainly still an I doing the living. The second is the letter itself. This is the most personality-drenched document in the New Testament; the man who wrote it is unmistakably himself on every page, angry, tender, sarcastic and affectionate by turns. Grace did not flatten Saul of Tarsus into a generic believer. It killed what he was living for and left him more himself than before.

What died was the self that had to be somebody. What lives is a man indwelt.

And the life I now live in the flesh — in the body, in ordinary circumstances, with a stomach and a temper and a tentmaking business. Not in some elevated spiritual condition. This is Monday he is describing.

I live by faith in the Son of God. Which is worth saying plainly, because people who love this verse sometimes expect it to feel like something and are troubled when it does not. Paul does not say he lives by a sensation of Christ’s presence, or by a continual awareness, or by spiritual experiences. He says he lives by faith — by trusting a person he cannot see, on days when nothing is felt at all. The indwelling is a fact about where Christ is, not a report on how the believer is doing.

And then the last clause, and Paul’s grammar goes suddenly singular: who loved me and gave himself for me.

He has spent the whole chapter on councils, delegations, apostles, mission fields, the terms of justification for the nations. And it ends here, with one man saying me twice. The cross is wide enough for the world and narrow enough to have a single name written on it. This is the same Paul who had been dragging women out of houses to prison.

Sit for a moment with what the Son of God has done. He loved — not the abstraction of humanity, but this particular man, with this particular record, while that record was still being written. And he did not send help; he gave himself, which is the only gift that costs the giver everything and leaves nothing in reserve. He had the Father’s glory and set it down. He had legions and did not call them. He went to a public execution for people who were his enemies at the time, and he did it gladly, and he would not be talked out of it. There is nothing in heaven or earth to set beside a love like that, and eternity will not be long enough to get to the end of it. (cf. Eph. 5:2; 1 John 3:16)

verseByVerse.quote: I do not nullify the grace of God, for if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with the sharpest sentence in it, and it is aimed straight at everyone who thought they were being the serious ones.

I do not nullify the grace of God. The word means to set aside, to annul — the term for treating a legal instrument as void. And it is almost certainly a charge being thrown back where it came from. Paul is the one being accused of treating God’s law as though it counted for nothing; he answers that it is the other side who are annulling something, and it is not the law.

Then the argument, and it is a single move, and there is no way round it: if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose.

Follow it slowly, because it is worth feeling the weight. Suppose there is any route to being right with God that runs through human obedience — any at all, even a small one, even as a supplement to grace. Then on that road God had a way of saving people that did not require the death of his Son. And in that case Calvary was not a rescue; it was the most appalling waste in the history of the universe. A Father watched his Son die in the dark for something that could have been managed another way.

That is the reductio, and it is why Paul’s temper in this letter is not disproportionate. The Judaizers thought they were adding a little rigour to a message that had gone soft. Paul shows them what their addition actually implies about the cross, and the implication is blasphemous. You cannot say Christ plus my performance without saying, underneath it, that his performance was insufficient — and the cross does not survive being called a supplement.

The phrase for no purpose is worth one more look. It means without cause, gratuitously, for nothing. Every religion of human achievement, however sincerely held, ends up saying that about the crucifixion, whether it means to or not.

Which is where the chapter has been going all along. It began with a private meeting and a man counting years, moved through a quarrel about a dinner table, and lands on the only thing any of it was ever about. If there had been another way, he would have taken it — he asked in the garden whether there was, three times, with his sweat falling like blood. There was not. The Son of God went to the cross because nothing less would do, and he went knowing exactly what it cost, and he did not die for no purpose. He died for sinners, and it worked, and it is finished, and there is nothing to add to it. (cf. Heb. 10:11–14)

3.title: The Promise and the Law: Abraham, Faith, and the Curse
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is the theological heart of Galatians: a sustained argument from Scripture that the gospel of grace by faith is not a Pauline novelty but the foundation on which all of God’s dealings with Abraham and his descendants have always rested. The law came 430 years after the Abrahamic covenant. It cannot therefore revoke the promise made to Abraham; it operates within a different register, serving a different purpose, pointing toward its own fulfillment and supersession in Christ.

Paul opens with an emotional appeal: the Galatians had experienced the Spirit. They knew it. Signs and wonders had accompanied their conversion. Did they receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith? The answer is obvious — and the answer settles the question about the ground of their acceptance with God. The same Spirit-receiving faith that initiated their Christian life is also the ongoing basis of their standing. Maturity in Christ is not a movement from faith toward law; it is a deepening of faith in the one in whom all the law finds its fulfillment.

The chapter’s christological climax is the most audacious claim in the letter: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us — for it is written, ‘Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree’” (v. 13). The cross was not merely a sacrifice; it was a specific legal exchange. Christ took the law’s curse — the curse pronounced on all who fail to keep it perfectly — onto himself, becoming the accused on behalf of the accused, so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles through Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul begins with one of the most rhetorical openings in his letters: “O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you?” The emotional intensity is pastoral urgency, not contempt. They had received a clear presentation of Christ crucified — Paul describes his preaching as a public placard of the crucifixion (“publicly portrayed as crucified”) — and they had experienced the Spirit in power. Now they are considering adding circumcision and law-observance to the faith they exercised when they received all of this. The absurdity is acute.

The six questions of verses 1–5 are not rhetorical flourishes but a logical argument: everything you received as Christians came through faith, not through law. The Spirit came by faith. The miracles were experienced by faith. If the beginning of your life in Christ was by faith, why would the continuation of it be by law? “Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh?” — the flesh here does not mean sinful desires but human religious effort, circumcision as a fleshly mark, the whole system of law-observance as a human contribution to what the Spirit has begun.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit Received by Faith

The argument from the Galatians’ own experience of the Spirit is not an appeal to subjectivism; it is an appeal to the epistemologically significant fact of how the Spirit came to them. The Spirit comes through the proclamation of the gospel received by faith — not through the performance of law-works. This is the experiential confirmation of the theological argument: the mechanism by which God gives the Spirit to his people is faith, not law. Reformed theology has consistently held that the Spirit applies the benefits of Christ to those who believe — the Spirit is the agent of union with Christ, and union with Christ is by faith. Law-works have no role in this transaction.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Galatians had undeniable experiential evidence that the Spirit came through faith: their conversions were accompanied by power, miracles, and obvious transformation. Paul asks them to think: did that happen when you did works of the law, or when you heard and believed the gospel? The question answers itself. Now: The testimony of every genuine conversion is the same: the Spirit came through hearing the gospel with faith. No one receives the Spirit through religious performance; performance cannot open the channel that only faith can open. The ongoing question for the believer is whether they seek the Spirit’s power by continuing in faith or by adding religious effort.

verseByVerse.quote: O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you? It was before your eyes that Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed as crucified. Let me ask you only this: Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith?
verseByVerse.commentary: “Bewitched” (ebaskanēn) — the image is of a malign spell cast by someone’s evil eye, drawing a person away from clear thinking. Paul cannot account for the Galatians’ movement toward the Judaizers’ gospel except as a kind of spiritual enchantment. Christ crucified had been “publicly portrayed” before them — the Greek suggests a public announcement placard, the kind used in the ancient world to display official proclamations. The cross was the content of Paul’s preaching, presented with clarity and power. How can anyone who has genuinely seen that cross then turn to law-keeping as the ground of their acceptance? The question about the Spirit is decisive: they know how they received it. And it was not by circumcision.

verseByVerse.quote: Are you so foolish? Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh? Did you suffer so many things in vain — if indeed it was in vain? Does he who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you do so by works of the law, or by hearing with faith?
verseByVerse.commentary: “Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh?” — this is the logic of the Galatian error exposed. They did not begin their Christian life by doing works of the law; they began it by receiving the Spirit through faith. Now the Judaizers are suggesting that they must advance beyond that beginning by adding law-performance. Paul says: this is regression, not progression. Moving from Spirit to flesh, from faith to works, from grace to performance is not spiritual maturity; it is spiritual foolishness. The miracles they had experienced — happening not through law-keeping but through faith-proclamation — were the evidence standing against the Judaizers’ position.

verseByVerse.quote: just as Abraham “believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness”. Know then that it is those of faith who are the sons of Abraham. And the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, “In you shall all the nations be blessed.” So then, those who are of faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith.
verseByVerse.commentary: The appeal to Abraham is the cornerstone of Paul’s theological argument. The Judaizers were claiming to represent the Abrahamic tradition. Paul shows that Abraham himself was justified by faith, not by circumcision (he was justified in Genesis 15, four chapters before the circumcision ordinance of Genesis 17). The true sons of Abraham are therefore defined not by circumcision but by the faith Abraham exercised. And the Abrahamic promise was always universal: “in you shall all the nations be blessed.” The gospel Paul was preaching to Gentiles was not a departure from the Abrahamic covenant; it was its fulfillment. Abraham’s blessing was always destined for the nations, always received by faith.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–14 — The Righteous Shall Live by Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having established that Abraham was justified by faith, Paul now establishes the negative counterpart: those who rely on the law are under a curse. The law itself says, “Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them” (Deut 27:26). The law demands comprehensive, perfect, continuous obedience. No one achieves this. Therefore, the law can only produce a curse for those who rely on it as the ground of their standing with God.

Then comes the magnificent exchange of verse 13: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us. He took the curse that the law pronounces on every lawbreaker — and every person who has ever lived under the law is a lawbreaker — onto himself. He “became a curse” by being “hanged on a tree,” fulfilling the pronouncement of Deuteronomy 21:23 that anyone hanged on a tree is cursed. The cross was not merely the site of his death; it was the legal mechanism by which the law’s curse was transferred to him and removed from all who belong to him. This is substitutionary atonement in its most precise legal form.
verseByVerse.theology:
Penal Substitution: The Logic of the Curse Exchange

The doctrine of penal substitution — that Christ bore the penalty due to sinners in their place, satisfying the law’s demands and exhausting its curse — is not a later theological development but the explicit content of Galatians 3:13. The exchange is legally precise: the curse that the law pronounces on lawbreakers fell on Christ on the cross, so that the blessing the law promises to the perfectly obedient could be given to all who are in Christ. This is not merely sympathetic solidarity (“he suffered with us”) but legal substitution (“he suffered instead of us, in our place, bearing our curse”). The Reformation’s insistence on penal substitution as the heart of the atonement is exegetically grounded here.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Judaizers were offering the Galatians the law as a supplementary means of securing divine blessing. Paul shows them that the law, far from delivering blessing, pronounces a curse on all who rely on it — because perfect compliance is the only condition the law accepts, and no one achieves it. The only exit from the law’s curse is the one who became a curse for us. Now: Every person who has ever tried to commend themselves to God by their moral performance has placed themselves under the law’s verdict: “cursed is everyone who does not abide by all things.” There is no partial credit. The law is binary: perfect obedience or curse. Only Christ met the first standard, and only Christ can absorb the second. Faith in him is the only exit.

verseByVerse.quote: For all who rely on works of the law are under a curse; for it is written, “Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them.” Now it is evident that no one is justified before God by the law, for “The righteous shall live by faith.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The law’s demand is comprehensive: “all things,” “abide by,” “do them.” There is no partial compliance; the law is a unity (James 2:10: “whoever keeps the whole law but fails in one point has become guilty of all of it”). To rely on the law as the ground of one’s standing with God is to submit oneself to this comprehensive demand — and to guarantee the curse, because no one meets it. Then Habakkuk 2:4: “the righteous shall live by faith.” Faith and law-reliance are mutually exclusive as the ground of justification. The righteous one lives by faith — trust in God’s promise, not achievement of God’s demand.

verseByVerse.quote: But the law is not of faith, rather “The one who does them shall live by them.” Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us — for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree” — so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us.” This is the theological apex of the chapter. The law and faith operate on different principles: the law says “do and live,” faith says “trust and receive.” Christ bridged the gap not by making the law’s demands easier but by meeting them perfectly on our behalf — and then absorbing the curse that our failure deserved. Deuteronomy 21:23 (“cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree”) was fulfilled at Calvary: the cross was the place of the curse, and Christ bore it. The result: the Abrahamic blessing (justification, the Spirit, adoption) flows to the Gentiles through Christ. The curse absorbed; the blessing released; the Spirit given. All through faith.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul now makes a legal-historical argument: a covenant, once ratified, cannot be modified by a later party. God ratified the covenant with Abraham — sealed it with a divine oath (Gen 15, 22) — and promised that the blessing would come through Abraham’s “offspring.” Paul makes the significant exegetical point that “offspring” is singular (“seed,” sperma), not plural, and argues that the singular points to Christ as the singular recipient of the Abrahamic promise. The Mosaic law, which came 430 years later, cannot annul this promise. It operates within a different register. The inheritance promised to Abraham is still received through faith in the promised Offspring, not through law-keeping.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Priority of the Promise

The covenant of grace — God’s unconditional promise to bless all nations through Abraham’s seed — is prior to and independent of the Mosaic law. This is one of the most important principles in Reformed covenant theology: the Mosaic administration does not replace the Abrahamic covenant but operates within it, serving it, without modifying its fundamental character as a covenant of promise received by faith. The Abrahamic promise was not conditioned on Mosaic law-observance; it was conditioned on the faithfulness of the Seed, who is Christ. The inheritance is therefore still received by those who share Abraham’s faith, in the same Seed Abraham believed in.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Judaizers were effectively arguing that the Mosaic law, given later, modified the conditions of the Abrahamic covenant. Paul shows this is legally impossible: a ratified covenant cannot be revoked or amended by a later addition. The law did not create a new way to receive the promise; it served the promise until the promised Seed arrived. Now: The argument that religious observance improves on or supplements the Abrahamic-covenant basis of salvation is as old as the Galatian crisis. Every generation needs to hear: the promise came first; the promise is in Christ; the promise is received by faith. Nothing adds to it.

verseByVerse.quote: To give a human example, brothers: even with a man-made covenant, no one annuls it or adds to it once it has been ratified. Now the promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring. It does not say, “And to offsprings,” referring to many, but referring to one, “And to your offspring,” who is Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary: The legal analogy is simple: a ratified will or covenant cannot be voided or amended by a subsequent party. God’s covenant with Abraham, once sworn and sealed, stands. Then the exegetical observation: “offspring” (sperma) is singular. This is not fanciful wordplay; Paul is drawing on an important feature of the Abrahamic promise — that the blessing would come through one particular heir, the Seed of the woman (Gen 3:15), the seed of Abraham, the son of David. The singular is ultimately fulfilled in Christ, the one Offspring who inherits all that God promised to Abraham and through whom all the nations receive the blessing.

verseByVerse.quote: This is what I mean: the law, which came 430 years afterward, does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to make the promise void. For if the inheritance comes by the law, it no longer comes by promise; but God gave it to Abraham by a promise.
verseByVerse.commentary: The chronological argument is decisive: 430 years separate the Abrahamic covenant from the giving of the Mosaic law. The law came after the promise, within the promise, in service of the promise — but it cannot supersede or modify a promise already unconditionally sealed by God. The two operate on fundamentally different principles: promise is unconditional and received by faith; law is conditional and demands performance. If the inheritance had come by law, it would no longer be a promise; if by promise, law-keeping cannot be its condition. God chose the promise; the law serves that choice without replacing it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–25 — The Purpose of the Law
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
If the law cannot justify and cannot nullify the promise, what is it for? Paul’s answer is precise and multi-layered. The law was “added because of transgressions” — to make sin explicit, to reveal its nature, to expose the depth of the problem that only the gospel can solve. It was “until the offspring should come” — temporary, purposeful, designed for a specific period in redemptive history. It was “put in place through angels by an intermediary” (Moses) — whereas the Abrahamic promise came directly from God, indicating the law’s subordinate status.

The metaphor of the guardian (paidagōgos) in verse 24 is the chapter’s most vivid image. A paidagōgos in the ancient world was a household slave entrusted with the oversight of a child — accompanying him to school, supervising his behavior, keeping him safe and disciplined. The slave was not the teacher; he got the child to the teacher. The law was Israel’s paidagōgos — not the source of life or justification, but the severe and necessary guardian that walked the nation through its childhood until Christ, the Teacher, arrived. Now that Christ has come, the guardian’s function has been completed: “we are no longer under a guardian.”
verseByVerse.theology:
The Law as Guardian: Temporary, Purposeful, Fulfilled

Reformed covenant theology has always insisted on the unity of the covenant of grace across both Testaments while acknowledging the distinct function of the Mosaic administration within redemptive history. The law’s role as guardian is an example of this: it was genuinely from God, genuinely binding in its time, genuinely serving the covenant of grace — but it was designed for a specific phase, not the final phase. Its abolition as a system of justification is not God changing his mind but God completing his plan. The law pointed to Christ; Christ has come; the finger can now rest.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Judaizers wanted to reinstall the guardian after the child had come of age. Paul says: the guardian was dismissed by divine design. To return to it is to misunderstand both the law and the gospel. Now: The Christian who tries to use the law as the ground of their standing before God is acting like a child who insists on being escorted to school after they have already graduated. The guardian served its purpose. Christ has come. Faith in him is the direct relationship for which the law was always preparing the way.

verseByVerse.quote: Why then the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made, and it was put in place through angels by an intermediary. Now an intermediary implies more than one, but God is one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Added because of transgressions” — the law was added to make transgressions explicit, to give sin its legal character as rebellion against God’s known command (Rom 5:13: “sin indeed was in the world before the law was given, but sin is not counted where there is no law”). The law revealed the depth of the problem: Israel’s history under the law is a record of repeated transgression against a clearly known standard. This revelation of sin was a gift, not a condemnation — it drove the nation toward the need for the Promised Seed. The mediation through angels and Moses signals the law’s subordinate status; the Abrahamic promise came directly from the one God.

“An intermediary implies more than one, but God is one” (v. 20) is famously compressed, but the thrust is clear. The law was a brokered arrangement — God, angels, Moses, Israel — a contract standing between parties and depending on both sides keeping terms. The promise was nothing of the kind: no broker, no chain, no second party to fail. The one God gave it to Abraham directly and unilaterally, resting on himself alone. A two-party contract can collapse; a one-party promise of God cannot — and that is why the promise stands above the law.

verseByVerse.quote: Is the law then contrary to the promises of God? Certainly not! For if a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would indeed be by the law. But the Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, so that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe.
verseByVerse.commentary: The law and the promise are not opposed; they serve the same purpose but in different modes. The law cannot give life — it was never designed to; its function is diagnostic, not curative. “The Scripture imprisoned everything under sin” — not arbitrarily but redemptively, so that there would be no other door, no alternative exit, no competing source of the righteousness that only the promise in Christ can provide. The imprisonment is grace: it closes every avenue of self-justification so that the only open door is faith in Jesus Christ. The law’s severity is the negative image of the gospel’s generosity.

verseByVerse.quote: Now before faith came, we were held captive under the law, imprisoned until the coming faith would be revealed. So then, the law was our guardian until Christ came, in order that we might be justified by faith. But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Before faith came” — Paul speaks of “faith” (pistis) both as a subjective act and as an objective era: the era of the new covenant, the age of the Spirit in which justifying faith is openly and fully available through the proclaimed gospel of Christ. The law held God’s people in a kind of protective custody during this period of waiting — kept them from total dissolution, kept sin’s nature visible, kept the need for a Savior urgent. Now the Savior has come. The guardian is dismissed. “We are no longer under a guardian” — this is not antinomianism (the law’s moral demands are fulfilled by those who walk in the Spirit, 5:14, 16), but it is the end of the law as the defining framework of the covenant relationship. That framework is now Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chapter concludes with one of the most revolutionary social-theological statements in the New Testament. In Christ Jesus, through faith, all who believe are “sons of God” — mature heirs of the promise, no longer minors under a guardian. The baptismal formula of verse 27 (“as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ”) grounds this new status in union with Christ: to be baptized into Christ is to be clothed in him, enveloped in his identity, defined by his status rather than one’s own.
